summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

primary_citations.citation_text: Louisiana - Children’s Code Article 601 et seq. (Children’s Code – Child in Need of Care, includes reporting duties)
Louisiana - Children’s Code Article 610 (Reporting procedure; which reports go to DCFS and which go to law enforcement)
Louisiana - Children’s Code Article 612 (Assignment of reports for investigation and assessment)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Todd v. State Through Department of Social Services, Office of Community Services
key_cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed judgments against a caseworker and the State for a child's suicide after an abuse investigation, holding the manner of investigation is discretionary and that the mother failed to prove the suicide was reasonably foreseeable or causally linked to the caseworker's conduct.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the discretion-versus-thoroughness test for an accepted investigation, including timeliness of the face-to-face contact.
key_cases.quote: The manner in which the investigation is conducted is one of discretion, unless the investigation is so incomplete that it could not be found to be thorough.

key_cases.case_name: Roe v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held that the plaintiffs raised a fact question whether the caseworker violated the child's Fourth Amendment rights, but reversed on qualified immunity because those rights were not clearly established, while holding the mother had consented to the investigative home visit and that silence cannot supply consent.
key_cases.relevance: Is the binding circuit authority on consent for the investigative home visit and interview that Louisiana requires under La. Ch.C. art. 612.
key_cases.quote: Although they still must obtain the parent's verbal, affirmative consent before conducting an investigative home interview, they need not obtain that consent again when they appear at the parent's doorstep.

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held that a child may not be seized from the home absent a court order, parental consent, or exigent circumstances, defined as reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse; the warrantless entry into the home was not justified, though the removal itself was reasonable on those facts.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that a warrantless entry to interview children is not justified by the investigative purpose alone.
key_cases.quote: there is reasonable cause to believe that the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse if he remains in his home

key_cases.case_name: Department of Children & Family Services in the Matter of Fregener Davis Henderson
key_cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court of appeal affirmed the administrative law judge's decision upholding DCFS's valid finding of neglect by dependency and the placement of the appellant's name on the State Central Registry, holding DCFS carried its burden by a preponderance of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Shows what a documented, thorough DCFS investigation looks like when tested on administrative review.
key_cases.quote: It has the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that its determination of a valid finding of child neglect by dependency should be upheld.

search_keywords: Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services

state_agency.name: Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services

investigation_requirements: DCFS investigates only where the suspected perpetrator is a parent or caretaker as defined in La. Ch.C. Art. 603 or falls within one of the additional categories in Art. 610(A)(1) (a person in an interpersonal dating or engagement relationship with the parent or caretaker, a person living in the same residence as the parent or caretaker or in any residence of the child, an early learning center or registered family child day care home operator or employee, another child residing in the same residence in a case of suspected sexual abuse, or an indeterminable perpetrator where the abuse is suspected to have occurred at the child’s residence); every other report is routed to a local or state law enforcement agency (La. Ch.C. Art. 610(A)(1)-(2))

On receiving a report DCFS must immediately assign a level of risk; high-risk reports are investigated immediately and intermediate-risk reports promptly, and the preliminary investigation must include an inquiry as to whether there is reason to know the child is an Indian child (La. Ch.C. Art. 612(A)(1)-(2))

In lieu of an investigation, reports of low levels of risk may be assessed through interviews with the family to identify needs and available matches to community resources; if the assessment shows the child is at immediate substantial risk of harm, the local child protection unit must immediately conduct an intensive investigation (La. Ch.C. Art. 612(A)(3))

Reports of sexual abuse in which the alleged perpetrator is a child may be assessed immediately through interviews with the family of the child victim and the alleged child perpetrator rather than investigated, with the same immediate-intensive-investigation trigger (La. Ch.C. Art. 612(A)(4); see also Art. 610(G)(5))
All interviews conducted in the course of a child protective investigation must be recorded (La. Ch.C. Art. 612(C))

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately for high-risk reports; promptly for intermediate-risk reports (statute sets no hour count)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Department receives the report and assigns a level of risk
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Violation of the duties imposed by Ch.C. Art. 612 subjects the offender to criminal prosecution authorized by La. R.S. 14:403(A)(2) (Art. 612(F))
